extracted.intended_audience: early-18th-century literate London readers; coffee-house society; readers and practitioners of theatre and manners
extracted.subtask_description: Short essays and observations aimed at evaluating stage acting, conversation, and social writing—giving normative guidance for actors, letter-writers, and conversational behaviour in early-18th-century urban society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of action for actors (Hamlet's directions)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Speak the speech as I pronounce it to you, trippingly on the tongue; but if you mouth it, as many of our players do, I had as lieve the town-crier had spoke my lines: nor do not saw the air too much with your hand thus; but use all gently: for in the very torrent, tempest, and, as I may say, the whirlwind of passion, you must acquire and beget a temperance that may give it smoothness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use natural, measured delivery: do not mouth words, do not over-gesture ('saw the air'), and in scenes of great passion preserve temperance so the passion has smoothness. The direction emphasizes clarity, moderation of gesture and voice, and a measured balance between feeling and control. Anti-patterns: 'mouthing' lines, excessive arm-sawing, tearing a passion to tatters, strutting and bellowing that produces imitation of humanity 'abominably.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Suit action to the word; word to the action
rubrics_metrics.description: “suit the action to the word, the word to the action; with this special observance, that you overstep not the modesty of nature; for anything so overdone, is from the purpose of playing, whose end... was, and is, to hold as it were the mirror up to Nature.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure physical action and vocal delivery are appropriate to the spoken text; avoid excess that violates natural modesty. The purpose of acting is realistic representation ('the mirror up to Nature'), so both speech and movement should cohere and remain believable. Overacting or underacting that breaks naturalness is critiqued. Examples/anti-patterns: overdone gestures, late or forced exits, acting that 'out-Herods Herod.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not overdo passions or 'split the ears of the groundlings'
rubrics_metrics.description: “Oh! it offends me to the soul, to see a robustious periwig-pated fellow tear a passion to tatters, to very rags, to split the ears of the groundlings...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive vocal force and histrionics intended to elicit cheap laughter or noise from the audience; such overacting pleases the unskilful but grieves the judicious. Anti-pattern: making noise and spectacle for crowds at the expense of truthful representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not allow clowns/fools to ad-lib beyond the written text
rubrics_metrics.description: “This should be reformed altogether; and let those that play your clowns, speak no more than is set down for them: for there be of them that will of themselves laugh, to set on some quantity of barren spectators to laugh too... that is villanous, and shows a most pitiful ambition in the fool that uses it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fools and comic performers should stick to the script; ad-libbing to provoke cheap laughter disrupts necessary business of the play and reflects poor taste/ambition. Anti-patterns: improvising jokes that derail plot or timing; seeking applause by needless interruptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of acting—hold the mirror up to Nature
rubrics_metrics.description: “...the end, both at the first and now, was, and is, to hold as it were the mirror up to Nature; to show Virtue her own feature; scorn her own image; and the very age and body of the time its form and pressure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acting should reflect and examine human nature and the age; performances are judged by their fidelity to human truth and their ability to reveal character and social conditions. Guidance: prioritize representational truth over mere spectacle or rhetorical display.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female history/writing: prioritize truth and simplicity over ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: “As to the faculty of writing itself, it will not, it is hoped, be demanded, that style and ornament shall be so much consulted, as truth and simplicity; which latter qualities we may more justly pretend to beyond the other sex.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When women write history or accounts concerning their own affairs, they should value truthful, simple narration rather than elaborate style and ornament. Emphasis on plainness and sincerity as virtues in writing; anti-pattern: prioritizing stylish rhetoric over factual simplicity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model for love-letters: plainness and sincerity; avoid affected rapture
rubrics_metrics.description: “I shall affect plainness and sincerity in my discourse to you, as much as other lovers do perplexity and rapture. Instead of saying, 'I shall die for you,' I profess I should be glad to lead my life with you...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courtship letters should favor straightforward, sincere expression over hyperbolic or overwrought declarations. Practical advice: be plain, avoid extravagant tropes ('I shall die for you'), and express reasonable, mutual motives for affection. Anti-pattern: ornate, exaggerated proclamations that obscure intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational manners: avoid superfluous discourse and voluble tongues
rubrics_metrics.description: General critique of conversational excess: persons guilty of 'superfluous discourse'—the whisperer without business, the laugher without wit, the complainer without receiving injuries, and a large crowd of impertinents whose tongues are too voluble for their brains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate conversational participants by relevance, wit, and restraint. Good conversation should be pertinent and measured; faults include needless whispering, laughter without substance, complaining without cause, and excessive loquacity. Examples: county squires who 'roar instead of speaking' and those who 'draw together parishes' by overly boisterous speech are criticized.
